data.text/html:
SQL basics, explained by touching it

An interactive companion to Asynk's video "SQL Basics Explained In 5 Minutes". The video builds a tiny books + authors database and then writes one query, keyword by keyword: SELECT … FROM … JOIN … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY … LIMIT. Its punchline: the order you write a query is not the order the database runs it. Here you'll build the same database and poke every keyword until that punchline feels obvious.

data.text/markdown:
1. Tables, rows, columns and keys

"Imagine a book. It has a title, a genre, a release date, a page count, an author. Each of these properties is called an attribute."
A table is the blueprint: the attributes become columns, every concrete book becomes a row. Two books can share a title, so each row gets a unique primary key (books.id). Authors have attributes of their own, so they get their own table, and books stores only the author's id: a foreign key (books.author_id → authors.id). Click a book to follow its foreign key; click an author to see every row that points at it.

data.text/markdown:
2. A query: SELECT … FROM … WHERE

"A query is a request to the database to retrieve or change data."
  • SELECT picks the attributes (columns) you want to see; * means everything.
  • FROM says which table to take them from.
  • WHERE tests every row against a condition. True → the row stays. False → it's gone. Conditions can use AND, OR, NOT, comparisons =, >, <, and keywords BETWEEN, IN, LIKE.
Build a query with the controls; the SQL text, the result, and the "every row gets tested" chart all update together.

SELECT title, release_year, pages
FROM books
WHERE pages > 350

data.text/markdown:
3. JOIN: gluing tables back together by matching keys

"For every book, find the author whose ID matches and merge them into one wider row."
The result of WHERE showed author_id = 3, not Stephen King. The name lives in the other table, so we join: 
SELECT b.title, a.name
FROM books AS b
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
Below is a mini version of both tables. Lines are matches of the ON condition. Switch the join type and watch which rows make it into the wider result: plain JOIN (= INNER JOIN) keeps only matched pairs; the OUTER variants also keep the lonely rows and pad the missing side with NULL.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='ROlb-0' random-id='d62f4f1a-6f1c-62a3-1d9a-b1e0e9ffe8ba'><marimo-anywidget data-initial-value='{"model_id":"646e19f7522a4da8b11693f575dfeb2a"}' data-label='null' data-model-id='"646e19f7522a4da8b11693f575dfeb2a"'></marimo-anywidget></marimo-ui-element>

SELECT b.title, a.name
FROM mini_books AS b
INNER JOIN mini_authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY a.name NULLS LAST, b.title

data.text/markdown:
Aliases: which id do you mean?

"Both tables have an attribute called id. So, which one do you mean?"
After a join the wide row has two columns called id. Asking for plain id is ambiguous, so the database refuses. Prefix with the table name (books.id), or give the table a short alias with AS (books AS b → b.id).

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='Vxnm-0' random-id='3e337006-adcb-3a78-91cc-9fb30c11c73f'><marimo-radio data-initial-value='"SELECT id, name …  (ambiguous)"' data-label='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003ePick a SELECT list\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-options='["SELECT id, name …  (ambiguous)","SELECT books.id, authors.name …  (full names)","SELECT b.id, a.name …  (aliases)"]' data-inline='false' data-disabled='false'></marimo-radio></marimo-ui-element>

SELECT id, name
FROM books
JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id
LIMIT 3

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eINNER\u003c/strong\u003e: the \u003cem\u003eDiary\u003c/em\u003e (\u003ccode\u003eNULL\u003c/code\u003e key) and \u003cem\u003eTerry Pratchett\u003c/em\u003e (no books) both vanish. 7 books in, 6 rows out.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLEFT\u003c/strong\u003e: the \u003cem\u003eDiary\u003c/em\u003e comes back with \u003ccode\u003ename = NULL\u003c/code\u003e. \u003cstrong\u003eRIGHT\u003c/strong\u003e: Pratchett comes back with \u003ccode\u003etitle = NULL\u003c/code\u003e. \u003cstrong\u003eFULL\u003c/strong\u003e: both.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eHover \u003cem\u003eStephen King\u003c/em\u003e: one author row matches two books, so his name is \u003cstrong\u003ecopied\u003c/strong\u003e into two result rows. That's how a join makes the result \u003cem\u003ewider\u003c/em\u003e and sometimes \u003cem\u003elonger\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4. Aggregation, GROUP BY and HAVING

"Aggregation functions take many rows and squeeze them into a single value."
COUNT(*), SUM(pages), AVG(pages), MIN, MAX collapse rows. Without GROUP BY the database doesn't know what to count for and fails. GROUP BY splits the rows into buckets, one per author, and the aggregate runs on each bucket separately. To keep only authors with more than five books you can't use WHERE; you need HAVING, which filters buckets instead of rows. Each square below is one book row, stacked into its author's bucket. Buckets that fail HAVING turn red.

data.text/html:
SELECT a.name, COUNT(*) AS value
FROM books AS b
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
2 bucket(s) survive

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWith \u003ccode\u003eCOUNT(*)\u003c/code\u003e and \u003ccode\u003e&gt; 5\u003c/code\u003e, only Christie (7) and King (6) survive, exactly the video's \"more than five books\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ePick \u003cstrong\u003eforget GROUP BY\u003c/strong\u003e and \u003cstrong\u003eWHERE instead of HAVING\u003c/strong\u003e: read the two errors. Both are explained by \u003cem\u003eexecution order\u003c/em\u003e (next sections).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSwitch to \u003ccode\u003eSUM(b.pages)\u003c/code\u003e and set the threshold to 1500: King's 3,291 pages win easily even though Christie has more books.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5. ORDER BY and LIMIT

"Order the output from the highest to the lowest number of written books… and if you want only the top 10, use LIMIT."
ORDER BY column ASC|DESC sorts the final rows; LIMIT n cuts off everything after the first n. That's the complete query from the video.

data.text/html:
SELECT a.name, COUNT(*) AS n_books, SUM(b.pages) AS total_pages, MIN(b.release_year) AS first_book
FROM books AS b
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.name
ORDER BY n_books DESC, a.name
LIMIT 3

data.text/markdown:
6. The twist: execution order

"The order of the keywords you just saw is the order you write, not the order the database runs it."
written SELECT FROM JOIN WHERE GROUP BY HAVING ORDER BY LIMIT
run FROM JOIN WHERE GROUP BY HAVING SELECT ORDER BY LIMIT
Step through the full query clause by clause. Both strips at the top show where you are: in the text you wrote, and in the database's real pipeline. The table is the intermediate result after that clause.

data.text/html: <marimo-ui-element object-id='TXez-0' random-id='d65f796c-cf81-0edd-59ed-05ee9c919a1d'><marimo-anywidget data-initial-value='{"model_id":"afb00596926d42858f4be281f861e226"}' data-label='null' data-model-id='"afb00596926d42858f4be281f861e226"'></marimo-anywidget></marimo-ui-element>

SELECT a.name, COUNT(*) AS n_books
FROM books AS b
JOIN authors AS a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.release_year >= 1900
GROUP BY a.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
ORDER BY n_books DESC, a.name
LIMIT 3
DuckDB's answer (matches the step-by-step replay: ✅)

Now you can \u003cem\u003esee\u003c/em\u003e why \u003ccode\u003eWHERE COUNT(*) &gt; 5\u003c/code\u003e is impossible.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003ccode\u003eWHERE b.release_year &gt;=\u003c/code\u003e to 1950: Christie's whole bucket disappears \u003cem\u003ebefore\u003c/em\u003e grouping, so HAVING never even sees her.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003ccode\u003eHAVING COUNT(*) &gt;\u003c/code\u003e to 6: only Christie (7) survives. Then also set the year to 1950: nobody survives, and an empty result is not an error.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cem\u003eNote: DuckDB is lenient and lets you reuse a \u003ccode\u003eSELECT\u003c/code\u003e alias in \u003ccode\u003eWHERE\u003c/code\u003e/\u003ccode\u003eGROUP BY\u003c/code\u003e as a convenience. Many databases (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) do not; the logical order above is why.\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
7. Sandbox: write your own queries

Tables available: books, authors (plus mini_books, mini_authors). Pick a challenge to load a starter, edit it, and press Run. Errors are shown, not hidden: reading them is half of learning SQL.

data.text/markdown: 8. Quiz: check yourself

data.text/html:
In a table, every row is a ____ and every column is an ____.
books.author_id pointing at authors.id is a…
Which clause does the database run FIRST?
You want authors with more than 5 books. Which keyword filters?
An INNER JOIN of books and authors keeps a book whose author_id is NULL.
Which runs LAST?
SELECT id FROM books JOIN authors ON … fails because…

data.text/markdown: Answer, then flip the switch.

Recap

Keyword Job Runs Works on
FROM pick the table 1 tables
JOIN … ON glue tables by matching keys (FK = PK) 2 rows of two tables
WHERE test each row, keep the TRUE ones 3 rows
GROUP BY split rows into buckets 4 rows → groups
HAVING test each bucket 5 groups
SELECT choose columns, compute aggregates, create aliases 6 columns
ORDER BY sort ASC / DESC 7 final rows
LIMIT keep the first n 8 final rows
Remember: you write SELECT first, but the database runs it sixth. Most "why doesn't this work?" moments (aggregates in WHERE, aliases in WHERE) are explained by that one table.
